entries.73d56a5d38b394f90cbe5c09849e626e414cb07d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8754" type="x-p"/> Then said all the trees unto the bramble - The word אטד atad, which we translate bramble, is supposed to mean the rhamnus, which is the largest of thorns, producing dreadful spikes, similar to darts. See Theodoret on <reference osisRef="Psa.58.10">Psa 58:10</reference>. There is much of the moral of this fable contained in the different kinds of trees mentioned. <div eID="gen8754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8755" type="x-p"/> 1. The olive; the most profitable tree to its owner, having few equals either for food or medicine. <div eID="gen8755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> 2. The fig tree; one of the most fruitful of trees, and yielding one of the most delicious fruits, and superior to all others for sweetness. <div eID="gen8756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8757" type="x-p"/> 3. The vine, which alone yields a liquor that, when properly prepared, and taken in strict moderation, is friendly both to the body and mind of man, having a most direct tendency to invigorate both. <div eID="gen8757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> 4. The bramble or thorn, which, however useful as a hedge, is dangerous to come near; and is here the emblem of an impious, cruel, and oppressive king. <div eID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> As the olive, fig, and vine, are said in this fable to refuse the royalty, because in consequence, they intimate, they should lose their own privileges, we learn that to be invested with power for the public good can be no privilege to the sovereign. If he discharge the office faithfully, it will plant his pillow with thorns, fill his soul with anxious cares, rob him of rest and quiet, and, in a word, will be to him a source of distress and misery. All this is represented here under the emblem of the trees losing their fatness, their sweetness and good fruits, and their cheering influence. In short, we see from this most sensible fable that the beneficent, benevolent, and highly illuminated mind, is ever averse from the love of power; and that those who do seek it are the thoughtless, the vain, the ambitious, and those who wish for power merely for the purpose of self-gratification; persons who have neither the disposition nor the knowledge to use power for the advantage of the community; and who, while they boast great things, and make great pretensions and promises, are the tyrants of the people, and often through their ambition, like the bramble in the fable kindle a flame of foreign or domestic war, in which their subjects are consumed. The sleepless nights and corroding cares of sovereignty, are most forcibly described by a poet of our own, whose equal in describing the inward workings of the human heart, in all varieties of character and circumstances, has never appeared either in ancient or modern times. Hear what he puts in the mouth of two of his care-worn kings: - "How many thousand of my poorest subjects <div eID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> Are at this hour asleep? - Sleep, gentle sleep, <div eID="gen8760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> Nature's soft nurse! how have I frighted thee, <div eID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> That thou no more wilt weigh my eyelids down, <div eID="gen8762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> And steep my senses in forgetfulness? <div eID="gen8763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> Why rather, sleep, liest thou in smoky cribs, <div eID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> Upon uneasy pallets stretching thee, <div eID="gen8765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> And hush'd with buzzing night-flies to thy slumber <div eID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> Than in the perfumed chambers of the great, <div eID="gen8767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> Under the canopies of costly state, <div eID="gen8768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> And lull'd with sounds of sweetest melody? <div eID="gen8769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> O thou dull god! why liest thou with the vile <div eID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> In loathsome beds; and leav'st the kingly couch <div eID="gen8771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> A watch-case, or a common 'larum bell? <div eID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8773" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou upon the high and giddy mast <div eID="gen8773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> Seal up the ship-boy's eyes, and rock his brains <div eID="gen8774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8775" type="x-p"/> In cradle of the rude imperious surge; <div eID="gen8775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> And in the visitation of the winds, <div eID="gen8776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> Who take the ruffian billows by the top, <div eID="gen8777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> Curling their monstrous heads and hanging them, <div eID="gen8778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> With deafening clamours, in the slippery clouds, <div eID="gen8779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> That, with the hurly, death itself awakes? <div eID="gen8780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> Canst thou, O partial sleep! give thy repose <div eID="gen8781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> To the wet sea-boy, in an hour so rude; <div eID="gen8782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> And, in the calmest and most stillest night, <div eID="gen8783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> With all appliances and means to boot, <div eID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> Deny it to a king? Then, happy low, lie down! <div eID="gen8785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown." - "O hard condition! twin-born with greatness, <div eID="gen8786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> Subjected to the breath of every fool, <div eID="gen8787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> Whose sense no more can feel but his own wringing! <div eID="gen8788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> What infinite heart's ease must kings neglect, <div eID="gen8789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> That private men enjoy! <div eID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> And what have kings, that privates have not too, <div eID="gen8791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> Save ceremony, save general ceremony?" - "'Tis not the balm, the scepter, and the ball, <div eID="gen8792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8793" type="x-p"/> The sword, the mace, the crown imperial, <div eID="gen8793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8794" type="x-p"/> The intertissued robe of gold and pearl, <div eID="gen8794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8795" type="x-p"/> The farced title running 'fore the king, <div eID="gen8795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8796" type="x-p"/> The throne he sits on, nor the tide of pomp <div eID="gen8796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8797" type="x-p"/> That beats upon the high shore of this world, <div eID="gen8797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8798" type="x-p"/> No, not all these, thrice gorgeous ceremony, <div eID="gen8798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8799" type="x-p"/> Not all these, laid in bed majestical, <div eID="gen8799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8800" type="x-p"/> Can sleep so soundly as the wretched slave." <div eID="gen8800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8801" type="x-p"/> Shakespeare <div eID="gen8801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8802" type="x-p"/> This is precisely the sentiment expressed in the denial of the olive, fig tree, and vine.
entries.fbcfdd4313d6beb32eeba1e3a83cee4320812e74: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen8802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8803" type="x-p"/> Come and put your trust in any shadow - The vain boast of the would-be sovereign; and of the man who is seeking to be put into power by the suffrages of the people. All promise, no performance. <div eID="gen8803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8804" type="x-p"/> Let fire come out of the bramble - A strong catachresis. The bramble was too low to give shelter to any tree; and so far from being able to consume others, that the smallest fire will reduce it to ashes, and that in the shortest time. Hence the very transitory mirth of fools is said to be like the cracking of thorns under a pot. Abimelech was the bramble; and the cedars of Lebanon, all the nobles and people of Israel. Could they therefore suppose that such a low-born, uneducated, cruel, and murderous man, could be a proper protector, or a humane governor? He who could imbrue his hands in the blood of his brethren in order to get into power, was not likely to stop at any means to retain that power when possessed. If, therefore, they took him for their king, they might rest assured that desolation and blood would mark the whole of his reign. The condensed moral of the whole fable is this: Weak, worthless, and wicked men, will ever be foremost to thrust themselves into power; and, in the end, to bring ruin upon themselves, and on the unhappy people over whom they preside.
entries.5b29e2317cca8ec3d1cad54a02c19c6dbd45a9e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen8804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8805" type="x-p"/> Let fire come out from Abimelech - As the thorn or bramble may be the means of kindling other wood, because it may be easily ignited; so shall Abimelech be the cause of kindling a fire of civil discord among you, that shall consume the rulers and great men of your country. A prophetic declaration of what would take place.
entries.cf871c663384a80610fd42b0256cf9b7f542e93d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8806" type="x-p"/> Went to Beer - Mr. Maundrell, in his journey from Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 64, 5th edit., mentions a place of this name, which he thinks to be that to which Jotham fled, and supposed to be the same as Mishmash, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.5">1Sam 14:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.31">1Sam 14:31</reference>. It is situated, he says, towards the south, on an easy declivity; and has a fountain of excellent water at the bottom of the hill from which it has taken its name.
entries.2d4ee853e8bb96d752d869fb68ad029d0f609f51: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen8806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8807" type="x-p"/> God sent an evil spirit - He permitted jealousies to take place which produced factions; and these factions produced insurrections, civil contentions, and slaughter.
entries.7659ec2851784841cd7e77c490a7c3ef4948271d: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen8807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8808" type="x-p"/> The men of Shechem set liers in wait - It pleased God to punish this bad man by the very persons who had contributed to his iniquitous elevation. So God often makes the instruments of men's sins the means of their punishment. It is likely that although Abimelech had his chief residence at Shechem, yet he frequently went to Ophrah, the city of his father; his claim to which there was none to oppose, as he had slain all his brethren. It was probably in his passage between those two places that the Shechemites had posted cut-throats, in order to assassinate him; as such men had no moral principle, they robbed and plundered all who came that way.
entries.7a4da1a3ac7e9d140d1f89988c0fc3c4333d22be: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen8808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8809" type="x-p"/> Gaal the son of Ebed - Of this person we know no more than is here told. He was probably one of the descendants of the Canaanites, who hoped from the state of the public mind, and their disaffection to Abimelech, to cause a revolution, and thus to restore the ancient government as it was under Hamor, the father of Shechem.
entries.9beebe4d047f2575081169858269c23afde5c1b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen8809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8810" type="x-p"/> Zebul his officer - פקידו pekido, his overseer; probably governor of Shechem in his absence.
entries.efc2bb7087cbffdd6504ed291935d2824e1619d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen8810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8811" type="x-p"/> Would to God this people were under my hand - The very words and conduct of a sly, hypocritical demagogue. <div eID="gen8811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8812" type="x-p"/> Increase thine army, and come out - When he found his party strong, and the public feeling warped to his side, then he appears to have sent a challenge to Abimelech, to come out and fight him.
entries.8ac13a1bebe1094b528591f4cd867b5ca1d073ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen8812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8813" type="x-p"/> They fortify the city against thee - Under pretense of repairing the walls and towers, they were actually putting the place in a state of defense, intending to seize on the government as soon as they should find Abimelech coming against them. Fortifying the city may mean seducing the inhabitants from their loyalty to Abimelech.
entries.fc08290ae8f37c04a47ae458514e5010b3dc1542: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen8813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8814" type="x-p"/> Stood in the entering of the gate - Having probably got some intimation of the designs of Zebul and Abimelech.
entries.6c4e7fcea8771d8e50bf1ff645c8bcbfc233662b: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen8814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8815" type="x-p"/> By the plain of Meonenim - Some translate, by the way of the oaks, or oaken groves; others, by the way of the magicians, or regarders of the times, as in our margin. Probably it was a place in which augurs and soothsayers dwelt.
entries.d9bec6ef8e4716574a3455c147f46b6d76d22399: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen8815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8816" type="x-p"/> And sowed it with salt - Intending that the destruction of this city should be a perpetual memorial of his achievements. The salt was not designed to render it barren, as some have imagined; for who would think of cultivating a city? but as salt is an emblem of incorruption and perpetuity, it was no doubt designed to perpetuate the memorial of this transaction, and as a token that he wished this desolation to be eternal. This sowing a place with salt was a custom in different nations to express permanent desolation and abhorrence. Sigonius observes that when the city of Milan was taken, in a.d. 1162, the walls were razed, and it was sown with salt. And Brantome informs us that it was ancient custom in France to sow the house of a man with salt, who had been declared a traitor to his king. Charles IX., king of France, the most base and perfidious of human beings, caused the house of the Admiral Coligni (whom he and the Duke of Guise caused to be murdered, with thousands more of Protestants, on the eve of St. Bartholomew, 1572) to be sown with salt! How many houses have been since sown with salt in France by the just judgments of God, in revenge for the massacre of the Protestants on the eve of St. Bartholomew! Yet for all this God's wrath is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.
entries.de6f815f17a7f173890dfa01719548b7956eb8ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen8816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8817" type="x-p"/> A hold of the house of the god Berith - This must mean the precincts of the temple, as we find there were a thousand men and women together in that place.
entries.f2d655585ba07d5d3326c465acb93e6824d2ce96: <hi type="bold">Verse 53</hi> <div eID="gen8817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8818" type="x-p"/> A piece of a millstone - פלח רכב pelach recheb, a piece of a chariot wheel; but the word is used in other places for upper millstones, and is so understood here by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. <div eID="gen8818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8819" type="x-p"/> And all to break his skull - A most nonsensical version of ותרץ את גלגלתו vattarits eth gulgolto, which is literally, And she brake, or fractured, his skull. Plutarch, in his life of Pyrrhus, observes that this king was killed at the siege of Thebes, by a piece of a tile, which a woman threw upon his head.
entries.f23aad40c3ee29a16e87e545cc3ca0b1b142127a: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen8819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8820" type="x-p"/> Draw thy sword, and slay me - It was a disgrace to be killed by a woman; on this account, Seneca the tragedian deplores the death of Hercules: - <div eID="gen8820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8821" type="x-p"/> O turpe fatum! femina Herculeae necis <div eID="gen8821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8822" type="x-p"/> Autor feritur. <div eID="gen8822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8823" type="x-p"/> Herc. Oetaeus, ver. 1177. "O dishonorable fate! a woman is reported to have been author of the death of Hercules." <div eID="gen8823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8824" type="x-p"/> Abimelech was also afraid that if he fell thus mortally wounded into the hands of his enemies they might treat him with cruelty and insult.
entries.4b7031a4b72d79c8f72b8990a4e7b20a80d896f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 56</hi> <div eID="gen8824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8825" type="x-p"/> Thus God rendered, etc. - Both the fratricide Abimelech, and the unprincipled men of Shechem, had the iniquity visited upon them of which they had been guilty. Man's judgment may be avoided; but there is no escape from the judgments of God. <div eID="gen8825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8826" type="x-p"/> I Have said that the fable of Jotham is the oldest, and perhaps the best, in the world; and referred for other particulars to the end of the chapter. <div eID="gen8826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8827" type="x-p"/> On the general subject of fable, apologue, and parable, the reader will find a considerable dissertation at the end of <reference osisRef="Mat.13.58">Mat 13:58</reference>; I shall add but a few things here, and they shall refer to the oldest collection of fables extant. These are of Indian origin, and are preserved in the Sanscreet, from which they have been translated into different languages, both Asiatic and European, under various titles. The collection is called Hitopadesa, and the author Veshnoo Sarma; but they are known in Europe by The Tales and Fables of Bidpay, or Pilpay, an ancient Indian Philosopher. Of this collection Sir William Jones takes the following notice: - "The fables of Veshnoo Sarma, whom we ridiculously call Pilpay, are the most beautiful, if not the most ancient, collection of apologues in the world. They were first translated from the Sanscreet, in the sixth century, by Buzerchumihr, or bright as the sun, the chief physician, and afterwards the vizir of the great Anushirwan; and are extant under various names, in more than twenty languages. But their original title is Hitopadesa, or amicable instruction; and as the very existence of Aesop, whom the Arabs believe to have been an Abyssinian, appears rather doubtful, I am not disinclined to suppose that the first moral fables which appeared in Europe were of Indian or Aethiopian origin." <div eID="gen8827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8828" type="x-p"/> Mr. Frazer, in his collection of Oriental MSS. at the end of his History of Nadir Shah, gives us the following account of this curious and instructive work: - "The ancient brahmins of India, after a good deal of time and labor, compiled a treatise, (which they called Kurtuk Dumnik), in which were inserted the choicest treasure of wisdom and the most perfect rules for governing a people. This book they presented to their rajahs, who kept it with the greatest secrecy and care. About the time of Mohammed's birth or the latter end of the sixth century, Noishervan the Just, who then reigned in Persia, discovered a great inclination to see that book; for which purpose Burzuvia, a physician, who had a surprising talent in learning several languages, particularly Sanskerritt, was introduced to him as the most proper person to be employed to get a copy of it. He went to India, where, after some years' stay, and great trouble, he procured it. It was translated into the Pehluvi (the ancient Persian language) by him and Buzrjumehr, the vizir. Noishervan, ever after, and all his successors, the Persian kings, had this book in high esteem, and took the greatest care to keep it secret. At last Abu Jaffer Munsour zu Nikky, who was the second caliph of the Abassi reign, by great search got a copy of it in the Pehluvi language, and ordered Imam Hassan Abdal Mokaffa, who was the most learned of the age, to translate it into Arabic. This prince ever after made it his guide, not only in affairs relating to the government, but also in private life. "In the year 380 of the Hegira, Sultan Mahmud Ghazi put into verse; and afterwards, in the year 515, by order of Bheram Shah ben Massaud, that which Abdal Mokaffa had translated was retranslated into Persic by Abdul Mala Nasser Allah Mustofi; and this is that Kulila Dumna which is now extant. As this latter had too many Arabic verses and obsolete phrases in it, Molana Ali beg Hessein Vaes, at the request of Emir Soheli, keeper of the seals to Sultan Hossein Mirza, put it into a more modern style, and gave it the title of Anuar Soheli. "In the year 1002, the great moghul Jalal o Din Mohommed Akbar ordered his own secretary and vizir, the learned Abul Fazl, to illustrate the obscure passages, abridge the long digressions, and put it into such a style as would be most familiar to all capacities; which he accordingly did, and gave it the name of Ayar Danish, or the Criterion of Wisdom." This far Mr. Frazer, under the word Ayar Danish. "In the year 1709," says Dr. Wilkins, "the Kulila Dumna, the Persian version of Abul Mala Nasser Allah Mustofi, made in the 515th year of the Hegira, was translated into French, with the title of Les Conseils et les Maximes de Pilpay, Philosophe Indien, sur les divers Etats de la Vie. This edition resembles the Hitopadesa more than any other then seen; and is evidently the immediate original of the English Instructive and entertaining Fables of Pilpay, an ancient Indian philosopher, which, in 1775, had gone through five editions. "The Anuar Soheli, above mentioned, about the year 1540, was rendered into the Turkish language; and the translator is said to have bestowed twenty years' labor upon it. In the year 1724, this edition M. Galland began to translate into French, and the first four chapters were then published; but, in the year 1778, M. Cardonne completed the work, in three volumes, giving it the name of Contes et Fables Indiennes de Bidpai et de Lokman; traduites d'Ali Tcheleby ben Saleh, amateur Turk; 'Indian Tales and Fables of Bidpay and Lockman, translated from Aly Tcheleby ben Saleh, a Turkish author.'" <div eID="gen8828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8829" type="x-p"/> The fables of Lockman were published in Arabic and Latin, with notes, by Erpenius, 4th. Amstel., 1636; and by the celebrated Golius, at the end of his edition of Erpen's Arabic Grammar, Lugd. Bat., 1656, with additional notes; and also in the edition of the same Grammar, by Albert Schultens, Lugd. Bat., 1748, 4th. They are only thirty-seven in number. <div eID="gen8829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8830" type="x-p"/> Of the Hitopadesa, or fables of Veshnoo Sarma, we have two very elegant English translations from the original Sanscreet: one by Sir William Jones, printed in his works, 4th., vol. 6, Lond. 1799; the other by the father of Sanscreet literature in Europe, Dr. Charles Wilkins, of the India House, 8 vo., Bath, 1787, with a collection of very important notes. <div eID="gen8830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8831" type="x-p"/> The Bahar Danush, or Sea of Wisdom, abounds with maxims, apothegms, etc., similar to those in the preceding works; this was most faithfully translated from the Persian, by Dr. Jonathan Scott, late Persian secretary to his excellency Warren Hastings, published in three vols. 12 mo., with notes, Shrewsbury, 1799. This is the most correct version of any Persian work yet offered to the public. The original is by Einaut Ullah. Of these works it may be said, they contain the wisdom of the oriental world; and many of the numerous maxims interspersed through them yield in importance only to those in the sacred writings. The fables attributed to Aesop have been repeatedly published in Greek and Latin, as well as in all the languages of Europe, and are well known. Those of Phaedrus are in general only a metrical version of the fables of Aesop. The compositions of La Fontaine, in French, and those of Mr. Gay, in English, are very valuable.  <chapter eID="Judg.9"/> <div eID="gen8831" type="x-p"/>

entries.a69230be935fae845339154f673b2921b4411643: Jdg 9:1-2 <div eID="gen3298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3299" type="x-p"/> Having gone to Shechem, the home of his mother (Jdg 8:31), Abimelech applied to his mother’s brothers and the whole family (all the relations) of the father’s house of his mother, and addressed them thus: “<hi type="italic">Speak, I pray you, in the ears of all the lords of Shechem,</hi>” i.e., speak to them publicly and solemnly. שׁכם בּעלי, the lords, i.e., the possessors or citizens of Shechem (compare Jdg 9:46 with Jdg 9:49, where מגדּל בּעלי is interchangeable with אנשׁי a; also Jdg 20:5, and <reference osisRef="Josh.24.11">Jos 24:11</reference>): they are not merely Canaanitish citizens, of whom there were some still living in Shechem according to Jdg 9:28, but all the citizens of the town; therefore chiefly Israelites. “<hi type="italic">What is better for you, that seventy men rule over you, all the sons of Jerubbaal, or</hi> (only) <hi type="italic">one man</hi> (i.e., Abimelech)? <hi type="italic">and remember that I am your flesh and bone</hi>” (blood relation, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.14">Gen 29:14</reference>). The name “sons of Jerubbaal,” i.e., of the man who had destroyed the altar of Baal, was just as little adapted to commend the sons of Gideon to the Shechemites, who were devoted to the worship of Baal, as the remark that seventy men were to rule over them. No such rule ever existed, or was even aspired to by the seventy sons of Gideon. But Abimelech assumed that his brothers possessed the same thirst for ruling as he did himself; and the citizens of Shechem might be all the more ready to put faith in his assertions, since the distinction which Gideon had enjoyed was thoroughly adapted to secure a prominent place in the nation for his sons.
entries.cf2618281db583df6da43675a3f4cb84bd5a979c: Jdg 9:3 <div eID="gen3299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3300" type="x-p"/> When his mother’s brethren spake to the citizens of Shechem concerning him, i.e., respecting him and his proposal, their heart turned to Abimelech.
entries.6189149f90d64114ebdbfe56d45f8775ddb2f3ba: Jdg 9:4-5 <div eID="gen3300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3301" type="x-p"/> They gave him seventy shekels of silver from the house of Baal-berith, i.e., from the treasury of the temple that was dedicated to the covenant Baal at Shechem, as temple treasures were frequently applied to political purposes (see 1Ki 15:18). With this money Abimelech easily hired light and desperate men, who followed him (attached themselves to him); and with their help he murdered his brethren at Ophrah, seventy men, with the exception of Jotham the youngest, who had hidden himself. The number seventy, the total number of his brethren, is reduced by the exception mentioned immediately afterwards to sixty-nine who were really put to death. ריק, <hi type="italic">empty</hi>, i.e., without moral restraint. פּחז <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. gurgling up, boiling over; figuratively, <hi type="italic">hot</hi>, <hi type="italic">desperate men</hi>. “<hi type="italic">Upon</hi> (against) <hi type="italic">one stone</hi>,” that is to say, by a formal execution: a bloody omen of the kingdom of ten tribes, which was afterwards founded at Shechem by the Ephraimite Jeroboam, in which one dynasty overthrew another, and generally sought to establish its power by exterminating the whole family of the dynasty that had been overthrown (see 1Ki 15:27., 2Ki 10:1.). Even in Judah, Athaliah the worshipper of Baal sought to usurp the government by exterminating the whole of the descendants of her son (2 Kings 11). Such fratricides have also occurred in quite recent times in the Mohammedan countries of the East.
entries.accb16bd32f9038d803a192c352072fb558eb9ed: Jdg 9:6 <div eID="gen3301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3302" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Then all the citizens of Shechem assembled together, and all the house of Millo, and made Abimelech king at the memorial terebinth at Shechem.</hi>” <hi type="italic">Millo</hi> is unquestionably the name of the castle or citadel of the town of Shechem, which is called the tower of Shechem in Jdg 9:46-49. The word <hi type="italic">Millo</hi> (Chaldee מלּיתא) signifies primarily a rampart, inasmuch as it consisted of two walls, with the space between them filled with rubbish. There was also a <hi type="italic">Millo</hi> at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.9">2Sa 5:9</reference>; 1Ki 9:15). “<hi type="italic">All the house of Millo</hi>” are all the inhabitants of the castle, the same persons who are described in Jdg 9:46 as “all the men (<hi type="italic">baale</hi>) of the tower.” The meaning of מצּב אלון is doubtful. מצּב, the thing set up, is a military post in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.3">Isa 29:3</reference>; but it may also mean a monument of memorial, and here it probably denotes the large stone set up as a memorial at Shechem under the oak or terebinth (see <reference osisRef="Gen.35.4">Gen 35:4</reference>). The inhabitants of Shechem, the worshippers of Baal-berith, carried out the election of Abimelech as king in the very same place in which Joshua had held the last national assembly, and had renewed the covenant of Israel with Jehovah the true covenant God (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.1">Jos 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.25-Josh.24.26">Jos 24:25-26</reference>). It was there in all probability that the temple of Baal-berith was to be found, namely, according to Jdg 9:46, near the tower of Shechem or the citadel of Millo.
entries.60f1fafb05a68caed03a8c549f2f5317efd4752e: Jdg 9:7-15 <div eID="gen3302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3303" type="x-p"/> When Jotham, who had escaped after the murder, was told of the election which had taken place, he went to the top of Mount Gerizim, which rises as a steep wall of rock to the height of about 800 feet above the valley of Shechem on the south side of the city (<hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. iii. p. 96), and cried with a loud voice, “<hi type="italic">Hearken to me, ye lords of Shechem, and God will also hearken to you</hi>.” After this appeal, which calls to mind the language of the prophets, he uttered aloud a fable of the trees which wanted to anoint a king over them-a fable of true prophetic significance, and the earliest with which we are acquainted (Jdg 9:8-15). To the appeal which is made to them in succession to become king over the trees, the olive tree, the fig tree, and the vine all reply: Shall we give up our calling, to bear valuable fruits for the good and enjoyment of God and men, and soar above the other trees? The briar, however, to which the trees turn last of all, is delighted at the unexpected honour that is offered it, and says, “<hi type="italic">Will ye in truth anoint me king over you? Then come and trust in my shadow; but if not, let fire go out of the briar and consume the cedars of Lebanon.</hi>” The rare form מלוכה (<hi type="italic">Chethib</hi>, Jdg 9:8, Jdg 9:12) also occurs in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">1Sa 28:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.11">Isa 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.2">Psa 26:2</reference> : see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §228, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). מלכי (Jdg 9:10) is also rare (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §226, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The form החדלתּי (Jdg 9:9, Jdg 9:11, Jdg 9:13), which is quite unique, is not “<hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> or <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>, compounded of ההחד or ההחד” (<hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §51, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), for neither the <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> nor the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> of חדל occurs anywhere else; but it is a simple <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, and the obscure <hi type="italic">o</hi> sound is chosen instead of the <hi type="italic">a</hi> sound for the sake of euphony, i.e., to assist the pronunciation of the guttural syllables which follow one after another. The meaning of the fable is very easy to understand. The olive tree, fig tree, and vine do not represent different historical persons, such as the judges Othniel, Deborah, and Gideon, as the Rabbins affirm, but in a perfectly general way the nobler families or persons who bring forth fruit and blessing in the calling appointed them by God, and promote the prosperity of the people and kingdom in a manner that is well-pleasing to God and men. Oil, figs, and wine were the most valuable productions of the land of Canaan, whereas the briar was good for nothing but to burn. The noble fruit-trees would not tear themselves from the soil in which they had been planted and had borne fruit, to soar (נוּע, float about) above the trees, i.e., not merely to rule over the trees, but<hi type="italic">obire et circumagi in rebus eorum curandis</hi>. נוּע includes the idea of restlessness and insecurity of existence. The explanation given in the <hi type="italic">Berleb</hi>. Bible, “We have here what it is to be a king, to reign or be lord over many others, namely, very frequently to do nothing else than float about in such restlessness and distraction of thoughts, feelings, and desires, that very little good or sweet fruit ever falls to the ground,” if not a truth without exception so far as royalty is concerned, is at all events perfectly true in relation to what Abimelech aimed at and attained, to be a king by the will of the people and not by the grace of God. Wherever the Lord does not found the monarchy, or the king himself does not lay the foundations of his government in God and the grace of God, he is never anything but a tree, moving about above other trees without a firm root in a fruitful soil, utterly unable to bear fruit to the glory of God and the good of men. The expression “<hi type="italic">all the trees</hi>” is to be carefully noticed in Jdg 9:14. “<hi type="italic">All the trees</hi>” say to the briar, Be king over us, whereas in the previous verse only “<hi type="italic">the </hi>trees” are mentioned. This implies that of all the trees not one was willing to be king himself, but that they were unanimous in transferring the honour to the briar. The briar, which has nothing but thorns upon it, and does not even cast sufficient shadow for any one to lie down in its shadow and protect himself from the burning heat of the sun, is an admirable simile for a worthless man, who can do nothing but harm. The words of the briar, “<hi type="italic">Trust in my shadow,</hi>” seek refuge there, contain a deep irony, the truth of which the Shechemites were very soon to discover. “<hi type="italic">And if not,</hi>” i.e., if ye do not find the protection you expect, fire will go out of the briar and consume the cedars of Lebanon, the largest and noblest trees. Thorns easily catch fire (see <reference osisRef="Exod.22.5">Exo 22:5</reference>). The most insignificant and most worthless man can be the cause of harm to the mightiest and most distinguished. <div eID="gen3303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3304" type="x-p"/> In Jdg 9:16-20 Jotham gives the application of his fable, for there was no necessity for any special explanation of it, since it was perfectly clear and intelligible in itself. These verses form a long period, the first half of which is so extended by the insertion of parentheses introduced as explanations (Jdg 9:17, Jdg 9:18), that the commencement of it (Jdg 9:16) is taken up again in <hi type="italic">Jdg 9:19</hi> for the purpose of attaching the apodosis. “<hi type="italic">If ye have acted in truth and sincerity, and </hi>(i.e., when he) <hi type="italic">made Abimelech king; if ye have done well to Jerubbaal and his house, and if ye have done to him according to the doing of his hands ... as my father fought for you ... but ye have risen up to-day against my father’s house, and have slain ... if </hi>(I say) <hi type="italic">ye have acted in truth and sincerity to Jerubbaal and his house this day: then rejoice in Abimelech ...</hi>.” נפשׁו השׁליך, to throw away his life, i.e., expose to death. מנּגד, “<hi type="italic">from before him</hi>,” serves to strengthen the השׁליך. Jotham imputes the slaying of his brothers to the citizens of Shechem, as a crime which they themselves had committed (Jdg 9:18), because they had given Abimelech money out of their temple of Baal to carry out his designs against the sons of Jerubbaal (Jdg 9:4). In this reproach he had, strictly speaking, already pronounced sentence upon their doings. When, therefore, he proceeds still further in Jdg 9:19, “If ye have acted in truth towards Jerubbaal ... then rejoice,” etc., this turn contains the bitterest scorn at the faithlessness manifested towards Jerubbaal. In that case nothing could follow but the fulfilment of the threat and the bursting forth of the fire. In carrying out this point the application goes beyond the actual meaning of the parable itself. Not only will fire go forth from Abimelech and consume the lords of Shechem and the inhabitants of Millo, but fire will also go forth from them and devour Abimelech himself. The fulfilment of this threat was not long delayed, as the following history shows (Jdg 9:23.).
entries.201ed31e152060b6419a4b94f3149322cec732b2: Jdg 9:21 <div eID="gen3304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3305" type="x-p"/> But Jotham fled to <hi type="italic">Beer</hi>, after charging the Shechemites with their iniquity, and dwelt there before his brother Abimelech (“before,” i.e., “for fear of.” - <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>). <hi type="italic">Beer</hi> in all probability is not the same place as <hi type="italic">Beeroth</hi> in the tribe of Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.17">Jos 9:17</reference>), but, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s. v</hi>. Βηρά), a place eight Roman miles to the north of Eleutheropolis, situated in the plain; at present a desolate village called <hi type="italic">el Bîreh</hi>, near the mouth of Wady es Surâr, not far from the former Beth-shemesh (<hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. Pal. ii. p. 132). <div eID="gen3305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3306" type="x-p"/> Abimelech’s reign lasted three years. ויּשׂר, from שׂוּר to govern, is used intentionally, as it appears, in the place of ויּמלך, because Abimelech’s government was not a monarchical reign, but simply a tyrannical despotism. “<hi type="italic">Over Israel,</hi>” that is to say, not over the whole of the twelve tribes of Israel, but only over a portion of the nation, possibly the tribes of Ephraim and half Manasseh, which acknowledged his sway.
entries.ea45620a75a17d80af9bfb1eebce5186e30244df: Jdg 9:23-24 <div eID="gen3306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3307" type="x-p"/> Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem, so that they became treacherous towards him. “<hi type="italic">An evil spirit</hi>” is not merely “an evil disposition,” but an evil demon, which produced discord and strife, just as an evil spirit came upon Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.14-1Sam.16.15">1Sa 16:14-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.10">1Sa 18:10</reference>); not Satan himself, but a supernatural spiritual power which was under his influence. This evil spirit God sent to punish the wickedness of Abimelech and the Shechemites. <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, not <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, because the working of the divine justice is referred to here. “<hi type="italic">That the wickedness to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood</hi> (the blood of these sons that had been shed), <hi type="italic">to lay it upon Abimelech. </hi>” “<hi type="italic">And their blood</hi>” is only a more precise definition of “the wickedness to the seventy sons;” and “<hi type="italic">to lay it</hi>” is an explanation of the expression “might come.” The introduction of לשׂוּם, however, brings an <hi type="italic">anakolouthon</hi> into the construction, since the transitive שׂוּם presupposes <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> as the subject and דּמם as the object, whereas the parallel חמס is the subject to the intransitive לבוא: that the wickedness might come, and that God might lay the blood not only upon Abimelech, the author of the crime, but also upon the lords of Shechem, who had strengthened his hands to slay his brethren; had supported him by money, that he might be able to hire worthless fellows to execute his crime (Jdg 9:4, Jdg 9:5). <div eID="gen3307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3308" type="x-p"/> The faithlessness of the Shechemites towards Abimelech commenced by their placing liers in wait for him (לו, <hi type="italic">dat</hi>. <hi type="italic">incomm</hi>., to his disadvantage) upon the tops of the mountains (Ebal and Gerizim, between which Shechem was situated), who plundered every one who passed by them on the road. In what way they did harm to Abimelech by sending out liers in wait to plunder the passers-by, is not very clear from the brevity of the narrative. The general effect may have been, that they brought his government into discredit with the people by organizing a system of robbery and plunder, and thus aroused a spirit of discontent and rebellion. Possibly, however, these highway robbers were to watch for Abimelech himself, if he should come to Shechem, not only to plunder him, but, if possible, to despatch him altogether. This was made known to Abimelech. But before he had put down the brigandage, the treachery broke out into open rebellion.
entries.d81473450ea9e645512ada0543211196c0199dc5: Jdg 9:26 <div eID="gen3308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3309" type="x-p"/> Gaal, the son of Ebed, came to Shechem with his brethren. עבר with בּ, to pass over into a place. Who Gaal was, and whence he came, we are not informed. Many of the MSS and early editions, e.g., the Syriac and Arabic, read “son of Eber,” instead of “son of Ebed.” Judging from his appearance in Shechem, he was a knight-errant, who went about the country with his brethren, i.e., as captain of a company of freebooters, and was welcomed in Shechem, because the Shechemites, who were dissatisfied with the rule of Abimelech, hoped to find in him a man who would be able to render them good service in their revolt from Abimelech. This may be gathered from the words “<hi type="italic">and the lords of Shechem trusted in him.</hi>”
entries.3b168d41abdfa6d3736863f6f2544e0cd7e1ca98: Jdg 9:27 <div eID="gen3309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3310" type="x-p"/> At the vintage they prepared הלּוּלים, “praise-offerings,” with the grapes which they had gathered and pressed, eating and drinking in the house of their god, i.e., the temple of Baal-berith, and cursing Abimelech at these sacrificial meals, probably when they were excited with wine. הלּוּלים signifies, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.19.24">Lev 19:24</reference>, praise-offerings of the fruits which newly-planted orchards or vineyards bore in the fourth years. The presentation of these fruits, by which the vineyard or orchard was sanctified to the Lord, was associated, as we may learn from the passage before us, with sacrificial meals. The Shechemites held a similar festival in the temple of their covenant Baal, and in his honour, to that which the law prescribes for the Israelites in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23">Lev 19:23</reference>-25.
entries.693790d94f186cc3e1352b7cd241b7933577930c: Jdg 9:28-29 <div eID="gen3310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3311" type="x-p"/> At this feast Gaal called upon the Shechemites to revolt from Abimelech. “<hi type="italic">Who is Abimelech,</hi>” he exclaimed, “<hi type="italic">and who Shechem, that we serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem! and why should we, we serve him </hi>(Abimelech)?” The meaning of these words, which have been misinterpreted in several different ways, is very easily seen, if we bear in mind (1) that מי (who is?) in this double question cannot possibly be used in two different and altogether opposite senses, such as “how insignificant or contemptible is Abimelech,” and “how great and mighty is Shechem,” but that in both instances it must be expressive of disparagement and contempt, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.10">1Sa 25:10</reference>; and (2) that Gaal answers his own questions. Abimelech was regarded by him as contemptible, not because he was the son of a maid-servant or of very low birth, nor because he was ambitious and cruel, a patricide and the murderer of his brethren (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>), but because he was a son of Jerubbaal, a son of the man who destroyed the altar of Baal at Shechem and restored the worship of Jehovah, for which the Shechemites themselves had endeavoured to slay him (Jdg 6:27.). So also the meaning of the question, Who is Shechem? may be gathered from the answer, “and Zebul his officer.” The use of the personal מי (how) in relation to Shechem may be explained on the ground that Gaal is speaking not so much of the city as of its inhabitants. The might and greatness of Shechem did not consist in the might and authority of its prefect, Zebul, who had been appointed by Abimelech, and whom the Shechemites had no need to serve. Accordingly there is no necessity either for the arbitrary paraphrase of Shechem, given in the <hi type="italic">Sept</hi>., viz., υἱὸς Συχέμ (son of Shechem); or for the perfectly arbitrary assumption of <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>, that Shechem is only a second name for Abimelech, who was a descendant of Shechem; or even for the solution proposed by <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>, that Zebul was “a man of low birth and obscure origin,” which is quite incapable of proof. To Zebul, that one man whom Abimelech had appointed prefect of the city, Gaal opposes “<hi type="italic">the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem,</hi>” as those whom the Shechemites should serve (i.e., whose followers they should be). <hi type="italic">Hamor</hi> was the name of the Hivite prince who had founded the city of Shechem (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.19">Gen 33:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.34.2">Gen 34:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Josh.24.32">Jos 24:32</reference>). The “men of Hamor” were the patricians of the city, who “derived their origin from the noblest and most ancient stock of Hamor” (<hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>). Gaal opposes them to Abimelech and his representative Zebul.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi> maintains, though quite erroneously, that serving the men of Hamor is synonymous with serving Abimelech. But the very opposite of this is so clearly implied in the words, that there cannot be any doubt on the question. All that can be gathered from the words is that there were remnants of the Hivite (or Canaanitish) population still living in Shechem, and therefore that the Canaanites had not been entirely exterminated-a fact which would sufficiently explain the revival of the worship of Baal there.</note> <div eID="gen3311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3312" type="x-p"/> In the last clause, “<hi type="italic">why should we serve him</hi>” (Abimelech or his officer Zebul)? Gall identifies himself with the inhabitants of Shechem, that he may gain them fully over to his plans.
entries.57d2ec7bb7d108fcd9b262099a3d3860f1af37c0: Jdg 9:30-31 <div eID="gen3313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3314" type="x-p"/> This rebellious speech of Gaal was reported to Abimelech by the town-prefect Zebul, who sent messengers to him בּתרמה, either with deceit (תּרמה from רמה), i.e., employing deceit, inasmuch as he had listened to the speech quietly and with apparent assent, or “<hi type="italic">in Tormah</hi>,” the name of a place, תּרמה being a misspelling for ארמה = ארוּמה (Jdg 9:41). The <hi type="italic">Sept</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Chaldee</hi> take the word as an appellative = ἐν κρυφῇ, secretly; so also do <hi type="italic">Rashi</hi> and most of the earlier commentators, whilst <hi type="italic">R. Kimchi</hi> the elder has decided in favour of the second rendering as a proper name. As the word only occurs here, it is impossible to decide with certainty in favour of either view. צרים הנּם, behold they stir up the city against thee (צרים from צוּר in the sense of צרר).
entries.cd145a21e24571df97d4d669d424b2a8ba9473f0: Jdg 9:32-33 <div eID="gen3314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3315" type="x-p"/> At the same time he called upon Abimelech to draw near, with the people that he had with him, during the night, and to lie in wait in the field (ארב, to place one’s self in ambush), and the next morning to spread out with his army against the town; and when Gaal went out with his followers, he was to do to him “as his hand should find,” i.e., to deal with him as he best could and would under the circumstances. (On this formula, see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1Sa 10:7</reference>; 1Sa 25:8.)
entries.ee5b5114e52c846d91b78f23c3e099f0535c55db: Jdg 9:34 <div eID="gen3315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3316" type="x-p"/> On receiving this intelligence, Abimelech rose up during the night with the people that were with him, i.e., with such troops as he had, and placed four companies (“heads” as in Jdg 7:16) in ambush against Shechem.
entries.7350575298b83b80aa74cf7050fba032e1dcccb3: Jdg 9:35-36 <div eID="gen3316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3317" type="x-p"/> When Gaal went out in the morning with his retinue upon some enterprise, which is not more clearly defined, and stood before the city gate, Abimelech rose up with his army out of the ambush. On seeing this people, Gaal said to Zebul (who must therefore have come out of the city with him): “<hi type="italic">Behold, people come down from the tops of the mountains.</hi>” Zebul replied, for the purpose of deceiving him and making him feel quite secure, “<hi type="italic">Thou lookest upon the shadow of the mountains as men.</hi>”
entries.6d91c7d3d9ad0cef6ef4a32a7646a420a545d61c: Jdg 9:37 <div eID="gen3317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3318" type="x-p"/> But Gaal said again, “<hi type="italic">Behold, people come down from the navel of the land,</hi>” i.e., from the highest point of the surrounding country, “<hi type="italic">and a crowd comes by the way of the wizard’s terebinths,</hi>” - a place in the neighbourhood of Shechem that is not mentioned anywhere else, and therefore is not more precisely known.
entries.78a22660f7c87d59ec36d07a1e2f3f1e3acbdb34: Jdg 9:38 <div eID="gen3318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3319" type="x-p"/> Then Zebul declared openly against Gaal, and reproached him with his foolhardy speech, whilst Abimelech was drawing nearer with his troops: “<hi type="italic">Where is thy mouth now with which thou saidst, Who is Abimelech? Is not this the people that thou hast despised? Go out now and fight with him!</hi>”
entries.8fb6d370a0e73bc364be9e36fa7b759bf9ac95a1: Jdg 9:39-40 <div eID="gen3319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3320" type="x-p"/> Then Gaal went out “before the citizens of Shechem;” i.e., not at their head as their leaders, which is the meaning of לפני in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.3">Gen 33:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.21">Exo 13:21</reference>; Num 10:35, etc., - for, according to Jdg 9:33-35, Gaal had only gone out of the town with his own retinue, and, according to Jdg 9:42, Jdg 9:43, the people of Shechem did not go out till the next day, - but “in the sight of the lords of Shechem,” so that they looked upon the battle. But the battle ended unfortunately for him. Abimelech put him to flight (רדף as in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Lev 26:36</reference>), and there fell many slain up to the gate of the city, into which Gaal had fled with his followers.
entries.44e90b18ef41c575a51ddd4b115973b9c7db27cf: Jdg 9:41 <div eID="gen3320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3321" type="x-p"/> Abimelech did not force his way into the city, but remained (ישׁב, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. sat down) with his army in <hi type="italic">Arumah</hi>, a place not mentioned again, which was situated, according to Jdg 9:42, somewhere in the neighbourhood of Shechem. It cannot possibly have been the place called Ῥουμὰ ἡ καὶ Ἄριμα in the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. of <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi>, which was named Ῥέμφις in his day, and was situated in the neighbourhood of Diospolis (or Lydda). Zebul, however, drove Gaal and his brethren (i.e., his retinue) out of Shechem.
entries.851557249b25deab05b7d83528f831f6f0dc375a: Jdg 9:42-43 <div eID="gen3321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3322" type="x-p"/> The next day the people of Shechem went into the field, apparently not to make war upon Abimelech, but to work in the field, possibly to continue the vintage. But when Abimelech was informed of it, he divided the people, i.e., his own men, into three companies, which he placed in ambush in the field, and then fell upon the Shechemites when they had come out of the city, and slew them.
entries.2df4e584cd0b4936a43dd5d430d1ae4d8fb0e2fa: Jdg 9:44 <div eID="gen3322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3323" type="x-p"/> That is to say, Abimelech and the companies with him spread themselves out and took their station by the city gate to cut off the retreat of the Shechemites into the city, whilst the other two companies fell upon all who were in the field, and slew them.
entries.16dff2b878b2ce3bab2efba94eedd2419eff98cd: Jdg 9:45 <div eID="gen3323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3324" type="x-p"/> Thus Abimelech fought all that day against the city and took it; and having slain all the people therein, he destroyed the city and strewed salt upon it. Strewing the ruined city with salt, which only occurs here, was a symbolical act, signifying that the city was to be turned for ever into a barren salt desert. Salt ground is a barren desert (see <reference osisRef="Job.39.6">Job 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>).
entries.84b18537f0a3fa9b6b20197d745f9c449b95f35b: Jdg 9:46-49 <div eID="gen3324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3325" type="x-p"/> When the inhabitants of the castle of Shechem (“lords of the tower of Shechem” = “all the house of Millo,” Jdg 9:6) heard of the fate of the town of Shechem, they betook themselves to the hold of the house (temple) of the covenant god (Baal-berith), evidently not for the purpose of defending themselves there, but to seek safety at the sanctuary of their god from fear of the vengeance of Abimelech, towards whom they also had probably acted treacherously. The meaning of the word צריח, which answers to an Arabic word signifying <hi type="italic">arx, palatium, omnis structura elatior,</hi> cannot be exactly determined, as it only occurs again in <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sa 13:6</reference> in connection with caves and clefts of the rock. According to v. 49, it had a roof which could be set on fire. The meaning “tower” is only a conjecture founded upon the context, and does not suit, as צריח is distinguished from מגדּל.
entries.8d6ab931320f2245ff64623694e3e3d8129abcb2: Jdg 9:50-54 <div eID="gen3327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3328" type="x-p"/> He went from Shechem to Thebez, besieged the town, and took it. <hi type="italic">Thebez</hi>, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. thirteen miles from Neapolis (Shechem) on the road to Scythopolis (Beisan), has been preserved in the large village of <hi type="italic">Tubâs</hi> on the north of Shechem (see <hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. Pal. iii. p. 156, and Bibl. Res. p. 305). This town possessed a strong tower, in which men and women and all the inhabitants of the town took refuge and shut themselves in. But when Abimelech advanced to the tower and drew near to the door to set it on fire, a woman threw a millstone down upon him from the roof of the tower and smashed his skull, whereupon he called hastily to the attendant who carried his weapons to give him his death-blow with his sword, that men might not say of him “a woman slew him.” רכב פּלח, the upper millstone which was turned round, <hi type="italic">lapis vector</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Deut.24.6">Deu 24:6</reference>). תּריץ: from רצץ, with a toneless <hi type="italic">i</hi>, possibly to distinguish it from ותּרץ (from רוּץ). גּלגּלתּו, an unusual form for גּלגּלתּו, which is found in the edition of <hi type="italic">Norzi</hi> (Mantua, 1742).
entries.6b266ac3b2c62d13e6f30f6f132b26dfd52cbb69: Jdg 9:55-57 <div eID="gen3328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3329" type="x-p"/> After the death of Abimelech his army was dissolved. ישׂראל אישׁ are the Israelites who formed Abimelech’s army. In Jdg 9:56, Jdg 9:57, the historian closes this account with the remark, that in this manner God recompensed Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem, who had supported him in the murder of his brothers (Jdg 9:2), according to their doings. After the word “<hi type="italic">rendered</hi>” in Jdg 9:56 we must supply “upon his head,” as in Jdg 9:57. Thus Jotham’s curse was fulfilled upon Abimelech and upon the Shechemites, who had made him king.  <chapter eID="Judg.9"/> <div eID="gen3329" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Gaal the son of Ebed said, Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />melech <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">What is he but a base-born person, an Ambitious, Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perious, and Cruel Tyrant, and one every way unfit and unworthy to govern you?</ns0:note>, and who is Shechem <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="42">42 And it came to pass on the morrow, that the people went out into the field <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either, First, to renew the Fight, and avenge them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves for their last loss, the great God hardening their hearts to their Destruction, and the accomplishment of his Word delivered to them by <ns0:hi>Iotham.</ns0:hi> But here is not one word about the Peoples Arming, or Resisting, or Fighting, as there was before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 39. but only of their Slaughter, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 43, 44. Or, Secondly, to their usual, and then proper Imployments about their Lands: for though their Vintage was past, the Seed-time was now come, and other things were to be done in the Fields. Or, Thirdly, Upon some solemn occasion, not here expressed; possibly to make a solemn Procession, or perform some other Rites in the Fields, to the honour of their god <ns0:hi>Baal-berith,</ns0:hi> as the manner of the Heathen was, to make supplication to him for his help, and for bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter success; or onely to go for that end to the house of their god <ns0:hi>Baal-berith,</ns0:hi> which is thought to have been in the Fields; as may seem from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27, 46. on a Mountain upon the East side of the City.</ns0:note>, and they told Abimelech.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 And he took the people, and divided them in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to three companies <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Whereof he kept one with himself, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 44. and put the rest under other Commanders.</ns0:note>, and laid wait in the field, and looked, and behold, the people <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> come forth out of the city, and he rose up against them and smote them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 And Abimelech, and the company that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> with him, rushed forward, and stood in the entring of the gate of the city <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To prevent their Retreat into the City, and give the other two Companies opportunity to Cut them off.</ns0:note>, and the two <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />panies ran upon all <ns0:hi>the people</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> in the fields, and slew them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 And Abimelech fought against the city all that day, and he took the city, and slew the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> therein, and beat down the city, and sowed it with salt <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not to make the place barren, as salt will do, for then he would have sowed the Fields, not the City; but in to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken of his detestation and desire of their utter and irreco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verable Destruction: for Salt is the symbole or sign of Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />petuity; Compare <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 18. 19. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 29. 23. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 13. 5. <ns0:hi>Zeph.</ns0:hi> 2. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="46">46 ¶ And when all the men of the tower of She<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chem <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A strong place belonging to the City of <ns0:hi>Shechem,</ns0:hi> and made for its defence or security, but without the City. It is thought, this was that <ns0:hi>Millo</ns0:hi> which was confederate with <ns0:hi>Shechem</ns0:hi> in their design against <ns0:hi>Abimelech, v.</ns0:hi> 6. which also <ns0:hi>Iotham</ns0:hi> Cursed with <ns0:hi>Shechem, v.</ns0:hi> 20. and that Curse is noted to have its Effect, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 57. And this place may be called <ns0:hi>the Tower of Shechem;</ns0:hi> either because those who possessed and defended it, were sent from <ns0:hi>Shechem:</ns0:hi> Or, because it was built and kept for the safe-guard of <ns0:hi>Shechem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> heard <ns0:hi>that,</ns0:hi> they entred into an hold of the house of the god of Berith <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>Baal-berith, v.</ns0:hi> 4. Hither they fled out of the Town be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longing to it, fearing the same event with <ns0:hi>Shechem;</ns0:hi> and here they thought to be secure; partly by the strength of the place, as the Temples of Idols were oft-times built in the highest and strongest Places, as the Capitol at <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> and the Temple at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem;</ns0:hi> and such this place seems to have been, because they laid their Treasure here, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. Partly by the Religion of it, thinking that either their god would Protect them there, or that <ns0:hi>Abimelech</ns0:hi> would spare them there, if not out of piety to that god, yet out of thankful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness for the benefit which he received thence, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="47">47 And it was told Abimelech, that all the men of the tower of Shechem were gathered together<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> into that place.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 And Abimelech gate him up to mount Zal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">A place so called from its shadiness, because there were many Trees there.</ns0:note>, he, and all the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, and Abimelech took an ax in his hand, and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it, and laid <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> on his shoulder, and said unto the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, What ye have seen <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> I have done.</ns0:note> me do, make haste, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> do as <ns0:hi>I have done.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="49">49 And all the people likewise cut down every man his bough, and followed Abimelech, and put <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> to the hold, and set the hold on fire up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on them: so that all the men of the tower of She<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chem died also, about a thousand men and wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="50">50 ¶ Then went Abimelech to Thebez <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Another Town near to Shechem; and, as it seems, within its Territory.</ns0:note>, and encamped against Thebez, and took it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 But there was a strong tower within the city,
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:201" />
and thither fled all the men, and women <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">All that were not slain in the taking of the Town: or they all forsook the Town, and retired to their strong hold.</ns0:note>, and all they of the city, and shut <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to them, and gat them up to the top of the tower <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which was flat and plain, after their manner of Build<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="52">52 And Abimelech came unto the tower, and fought against it, and went hard unto the door of the tower, to burn it with fire.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="53">53 And a certain woman <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Sam. 11. 21</ns0:note> cast a piece of a milstone <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Such great stones no doubt they carried up with them, whereby they might defend themselves, or offend those who Assaulted them. Here the Justice of God is remarka<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble in suiting the Punishment to his Sin. He slew his Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren upon a stone, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. and he loseth his own life by a Stone.</ns0:note> upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="54">54 Then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">So 1 Sam. 31. 4.</ns0:note> he called hastily unto the young man his armour-bearer, and said unto him, Draw thy sword, and slay me, that men say not of me, A woman slew him <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which was esteemed a matter of disgrace.</ns0:note>: and his young man thrust him through, and he died.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="55">55 And when the men of Israel saw that Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />melech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="56">56 ¶ Thus God rendred the wickedness of Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />melech which he did unto <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Judg. 9. 5. Ruth. 4. 10.</ns0:note> his father <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">In rooting out, as far as he could, the name, and me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mory, and remainders of his Father.</ns0:note>, in slay<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his seventy brethren.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="57">57 And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham, the son of Jerubbaal.</ns0:p>
